claims.text: What the image looks like Wedge-shaped hypodensity respecting vascular territory → established/subacute ischemic stroke
claims.quote: Wedge-shaped hypodensity respecting vascular territory Established/subacute ischemic stroke

claims.text: Within 6 to 12 hours of ischemia, medium-sized to large infarcts start to become visible as hypodensities; small (eg, lacunar) infarcts may be visible only with MRI
claims.quote: Within 6 to 12 hours of ischemia, medium-sized to large infarcts start to become visible as hypodensities; small infarcts (eg, lacunar infarcts) may be visible only with MRI.

claims.text: Example CT: a large lucent infarction in the area supplied by the right middle cerebral artery
claims.quote: A large lucent infarction is seen in the area of brain supplied by the right middle cerebral artery.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Confirm it is non-contrast (so blood/calcium is not confused with contrast)
claims.quote: Confirm non-contrast (so blood/calcium not confused with contrast).

claims.text: Symmetry: gray-white differentiation, ventricles, sulci, basal cisterns
claims.quote: Symmetry - gray-white differentiation, ventricles, sulci, basal cisterns.

claims.text: Blood: look for hyperdensity 60-80 HU (epidural / subdural / SAH / IPH / IVH)
claims.quote: Blood - look for hyperdensity 60-80 HU (epidural / subdural / SAH / IPH / IVH).

claims.text: Brain: gray-white preservation; look for sulcal effacement, mass effect, midline shift
claims.quote: Brain - gray-white preservation, sulcal effacement, mass effect, midline shift.

claims.text: Cisterns: basal/suprasellar (5-pointed star); effaced = herniation risk
claims.quote: Cisterns - basal/suprasellar (5-pointed star); effaced = herniation risk.

claims.text: Ventricles: symmetric size; trapped temporal horn = early hydrocephalus
claims.quote: Ventricles - symmetric size; trapped temporal horn = early hydrocephalus.

claims.text: Causes Lacunar infarcts: small strokes (≤ 1.5 cm) in deep structures such as the basal ganglia, thalamus and pons, most commonly due to risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes; usual cause is lipohyalinosis of small perforating arteries; emboli may also cause them
claims.quote: Lacunar infarcts are small strokes (≤ 1.5 cm) that occur in deep brain structures such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, and pons. They are most commonly due to underlying risk factors for cerebrovascular disease such as hypertension and diabetes. The small infarcts result from nonatherothrombotic obstruction of small, perforating arteries that supply deep cortical structures; the usual cause is lipohyalinosis (degeneration of the media of small arteries and replacement by lipids and collagen). Emboli may also cause lacunar infarcts.

claims.text: Atheromas, particularly if ulcerated, predispose to thrombi; they are common at areas of turbulent flow, particularly the carotid bifurcation; thrombotic occlusion occurs most often at the main trunk of the middle cerebral artery and its branches
claims.quote: Atheromas, particularly if ulcerated, predispose to thrombi. Atheromas can occur in any major cerebral artery and are common at areas of turbulent flow, particularly at the carotid bifurcation. Partial or complete thrombotic occlusion occurs most often at the main trunk of the middle cerebral artery and its branches

claims.text: Symptoms Lacunar syndromes: pure motor hemiparesis, pure sensory hemianesthesia, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria–clumsy hand syndrome
claims.quote: Pure motor hemiparesis Pure sensory hemianesthesia Ataxic hemiparesis Dysarthria–clumsy hand syndrome | Lacunar infarcts

claims.text: Clues to stroke type: maximal deficits within minutes with embolic vs sometimes stepwise or slow onset with thrombotic; day (embolic) vs night (thrombotic); specific syndromes without cortical signs with lacunar infarcts (clinical differentiation is imprecise)
claims.quote: Although clinical differentiation is imprecise, some clues to help differentiate between common types of stroke include symptom progression (maximal deficits within minutes of onset with embolic versus sometimes stepwise or slow onset with thrombotic), time of onset (day with embolic versus night with thrombotic), and type of deficits (eg, specific syndromes and absence of cortical signs with lacunar infarcts).

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: antiplatelet, statin, etiology workup
Workup: test for cardiac causes (including atrial fibrillation) and arterial stenosis (with vascular imaging), and do blood tests as indicated
claims.quote: Test patients for cardiac causes (including atrial fibrillation) and arterial stenosis (with vascular imaging), and do blood tests (eg, for thrombotic, rheumatic, and other disorders) as indicated.

claims.text: To prevent future strokes: control modifiable risk factors and, when appropriate, use antiplatelet therapy, statin therapy and/or endarterectomy or stenting
claims.quote: To prevent future ischemic strokes, control modifiable risk factors and treat, when appropriate, with antiplatelet therapy, statin therapy, and/or endarterectomy or stenting.

claims.text: Acute antiplatelets reduce recurrent disabling stroke; options include aspirin 81 to 325 mg within 48 hours of onset, or aspirin plus clopidogrel within 24 hours for minor stroke or high TIA risk (ABCD2 score ≥ 4)
claims.quote: Oral antiplatelet medications are used in acute stroke treatment to reduce the risk of recurrent disabling stroke. The following may be used: Aspirin 81 to 325 mg within 48 hours of stroke onset Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel within 24 hours of stroke onset for patients with minor stroke or at high risk of a transient ischemic attack (TIA; ABCD2 score ≥ 4)

claims.text: Oral anticoagulants are indicated for secondary prevention of cardioembolic strokes, but contraindicated for thrombotic strokes
claims.quote: Oral anticoagulants are indicated for secondary prevention of cardioembolic strokes (as well as primary prevention), but are contraindicated for thrombotic strokes.

claims.text: Long-term management focuses on secondary prevention: treat hypertension, diabetes, smoking, alcohol use disorder, dyslipidemia and obesity
claims.quote: Long-term management focuses on prevention of recurrent stroke (secondary prevention). Modifiable risk factors (eg, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, alcohol use disorder, dyslipidemia, obesity) are treated.
